newsitem.title: CUBA: Castro tells "new rich" they must pay taxes.
newsitem.headline: Castro tells "new rich" they must pay taxes.

text.p: Cuban President Fidel Castro told citizens on Friday that the country's "new rich" -- self-employed people whose incomes are sometimes far more than wage earners -- must be made to pay taxes.

Castro said that failure to pay taxes was one example of "social indiscipline" that jeopardised Cuba's struggle to preserve its socialist system. He said allies of the United States in its bid to overthrow the Cuban revolution were "social parasites" and "people with no social discipline".

Speaking at an event to mark the 35th anniversary of the founding of the country's Union of Young Communists (UJC), the youth wing of the ruling Communist Party, Castro also criticised an illegal but common practice of people renting rooms or houses to foreign tourists.

He said such people should be made to have licences and pay taxes, although it was not clear whether he was preparing the ground for future legislation to make such private renting legal. Castro said there was a security danger to the unregistered renting of rooms to tourists, since foreigners might be "enemies" and authorities would not know where they were.
Castro noted that some people renting out property may earn as much as $600 a month, some 60 times more than the equivalent Cuban peso wage of an average worker.
Personal income taxes were reintroduced last year for the first time in three decades.

So far, the new income taxes have applied only to the small sector of the population that is self-employed, and to some Cubans working in cultural areas with dollar earnings abroad. Such Cubans had to file their tax returns for earnings in 1996 last month, and the national tax office has said most did file returns, although it is not clear how honest everyone was.

Castro noted that the self-emplyed, who include people running private restaurants or selling handicrafts, as well as those practicing trades, were sometimes earning up to 30 times more than wage earners.

He called the paying of taxes "an elementary moral duty" and questioned how the state was meant to pay for areas such as health and education without an input from taxpayers. "Are the Yankees meant to lend it to us, or what?," Castro said.

The Cuban leader noted, as he has done several times in the past, that the legalisation of self-employment in 1993 had not been a measure taken willingly but out of necessity as the country faced economic crisis and it was no longer possible for the state to guarantee 100 percent employment.

He expressed similar misgivings about other aspects of reforms of the early 1990s, including legalising the possession of dollars and having shops dealing in pesos and others dealing in hard currency, which he described as a "ghastly sacriledge".

The Cuban leader, 70, built his speech around a favourite theme, that while Cuba had enjoyed socialism in a "glass urn" while it had the alliance of the old Soviet Union and East bloc, it was having to learn to live without this and surrounded by "contaminating elements".
Cuban socialism did "not sink, it floated" despite the demise of the Soviet Union, he said. But Castro added that ensuring continued survival still meant an "arduous, long battle".
Such a battle depended on not just the country's economic progress but the "spiritual strength" of Cubans, he said.
